title: Vomiting and feeling unwell after overseas travel in a 35-year-old woman
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 35-year-old careers adviser in the ED. She has had about 10 days of malaise, fever, anorexia, right upper quadrant pain, dark urine and pale stools, and for the last 2 days vomiting, beginning a week and a half after she returned from backpacking in India without travel vaccines. The candidate then interprets her observations, blood results, hepatitis serology and malaria tests, and an upper abdominal ultrasound report. They give the diagnosis and differentials, outline ED management including public health notification, and safety-net before discharge.
focus: Vomiting in a returned traveller: taking a structured travel history, recognising acute hepatitis A, excluding malaria and acute liver failure, and managing it, including public health notification
stem: You are an intern in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital on a weekday afternoon. Leticia Moreno, a 35-year-old woman, has come in with vomiting. The triage nurse has taken her observations, put in an IV cannula and sent bloods. A nurse is with you and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from Leticia and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations, her blood results, her hepatitis serology and malaria tests, and an upper abdominal ultrasound report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting, and answer the examiner's questions (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Leticia Moreno, a 35-year-old careers adviser at a high school. You are lying on the trolley looking tired and washed out, with a vomit bag beside you. You are polite but flat, and you answer in short sentences. You are not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Give each detail only when you are asked about it. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I came back from overseas a few weeks ago and since then I've been feeling very ill, and now I have been vomiting for the past few days."

The vomiting (give only when asked)

  • It started suddenly 2 days ago.
  • At first it was partly digested food. You have not been eating much because you have no appetite, so now it is mostly clear fluid.
  • Only if asked: no blood and nothing like coffee grounds.
  • 3 times yesterday and twice so far today. It is not related to meals.
  • Nothing makes it better or worse. You are taking small sips of water but some comes back up.
  • "It feels like a very bad stomach bug."
  • You missed work yesterday and today.

Feeling ill since coming home (only when asked about each)

  • Malaise: about 10 days ago, roughly a week and a half after you got home, you started to feel exhausted and achy, "like the flu". You have had no energy since.
  • Fever: on and off for about a week you have felt hot and sweaty, then shivery. You have not taken your temperature.
  • Nausea and appetite: nauseated most of the time for about a week. You have gone off food completely, even coffee.
  • Pain: a dull ache under your right ribs for about 5 days. It is constant, about 4 out of 10, and does not go anywhere else. It is a bit worse if you press on it or the car goes over a bump. It does not come in waves and is not worse after fatty food.
  • Urine: dark, "like strong tea", for about 4 days. You thought you were just dehydrated. You are passing less than usual.
  • Stools: pale, "almost clay-coloured", for the last 2 to 3 days. Otherwise your bowels are normal and you are passing wind.
  • A little light-headed if you stand up quickly. You have not fainted.

Negatives (only if asked about each)

  • No yellowing of your skin or eyes that you have noticed. No itch. No rash.
  • No diarrhoea at any time.
  • No confusion or drowsiness. No nosebleeds, bleeding gums or unusual bruising.
  • No pain in the middle of the upper tummy going through to the back. No crampy pain after fatty meals. No pain that moved down to the lower right side.
  • No heartburn or reflux, no black stools, no vomiting blood.
  • No tummy swelling. You have never had an operation.
  • A mild headache with the aches early on, none now. No neck stiffness, no problems with your vision.
  • No cough, breathlessness or chest pain. No pain or burning passing urine.
  • Your periods are regular. The last one started 2 weeks ago and was normal. You have not been sexually active for more than a year, so you do not think you could be pregnant.
  • No diabetes. You have never had anything like this before.

The trip (only when asked)

  • Where and when: four weeks backpacking in northern India (Delhi, Rajasthan and several small villages) with a friend. You got back 3 weeks ago.
  • Accommodation: hostels and cheap guesthouses. Mosquito nets only some of the time.
  • Food and water: lots of street food, salads and cut fruit from markets, and ice in your drinks. You mostly drank bottled water but brushed your teeth with tap water. "I must have eaten something bad but I can't remember what."
  • Before the trip: you booked at the last minute and did not see a doctor or a travel clinic. No travel vaccines (so no hepatitis A vaccine) and no malaria tablets. Your childhood vaccines were done as far as you know.
  • Insect bites: quite a few mosquito bites. You did not always use repellent.
  • Other exposures: no sex while away or since. No tattoos, piercings, injections, medical or dental treatment, or blood transfusions overseas. No swimming in rivers or lakes. No animal bites or animal contact.
  • Sick contacts: your friend had one day of "Delhi belly" early in the trip and has been fine since. Nobody else you know is unwell.

Background (only when asked)

  • Past history: nil. No operations, no hospital admissions.
  • Medications: none, not even Panadol. No herbal remedies or supplements.
  • Allergies: none.
  • Family history: nothing significant.
  • Social: careers adviser at a high school. Never smoked. An occasional drink on weekends (if asked to quantify: 2 glasses of wine on a Saturday), none since you got sick. Never injected drugs. You live alone in a flat and are not in a relationship. You have friends nearby.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Idea: "It feels like a very bad stomach bug. I think I must have eaten something bad but I can't remember what."
  • Concern: "I thought I was just a bit under the weather or tired from travelling, but now that I've been vomiting, I'm a bit worried that this is more serious."
  • Expectation: something to stop the vomiting, and to find out what is wrong. You are also worried about more time off work.
  • Question to raise once in Part 1: "Could I have caught something serious over there?" A good candidate acknowledges the worry and says the tests will help answer it, without false reassurance.

The nurse and how Leticia changes

  • If the candidate asks for observations, the nurse gives the triage set: RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, BP 112/70, HR 104 regular, temperature 37.9 °C, alert, pain 4/10, BGL 5.4 mmol/L. Weight 62 kg.
  • Partway through the history, the nurse says: "She's just vomited again, about 150 mL of clear fluid, no blood."
  • If the candidate orders an antiemetic, the nurse gives it and a few minutes later Leticia says the nausea has eased a little. If IV fluids are ordered, the nurse sets them up.
  • If asked for a urine dipstick: dark amber urine; bilirubin 2+, ketones 2+, specific gravity 1.030; blood, leucocytes and nitrites negative.
  • If asked about a pregnancy test: "A serum beta-hCG went with the triage bloods. The result will come with the others."
  • If the candidate asks for blood cultures, the nurse takes them.
  • If the candidate orders any other treatment (anything other than an antiemetic or IV fluids), the examiner says: "Noted. Please cover your management in Part 2."
  • If the candidate asks for blood results, serology, malaria tests or imaging, the examiner says they will be given in Part 2.

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: tired and unwell, lying still, not distressed. Alert and oriented to time, place and person.
  • Observations: as the nurse's triage set above.
  • Hydration: dry mucous membranes. CRT 2 seconds, warm peripheries.
  • Eyes and skin: sclerae white in good light, no jaundice. No rash, petechiae or bruising. No tattoos or injection marks.
  • Hands and chest wall: no palmar erythema, clubbing, spider naevi or other stigmata of chronic liver disease. No asterixis.
  • Lymph nodes: no cervical, axillary or inguinal lymphadenopathy.
  • Abdomen, inspection: not distended, no scars.
  • Abdomen, palpation: soft. Mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant, no guarding, rigidity or rebound. Liver edge palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin, smooth, soft and tender. Murphy's sign negative. Spleen not palpable. No right iliac fossa tenderness. No masses.
  • Percussion and auscultation: no shifting dullness. Bowel sounds normal.
  • Renal angles: not tender.
  • Chest and heart: chest clear. Dual heart sounds, no murmurs.
  • Neck: no neck stiffness.
  • Rectal or pelvic examination: if offered, the examiner says it is not needed.

check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self, confirms Leticia's identity and gains consent for the history and examination.
Acknowledges that she is unwell and vomiting, offers or asks the nurse for an antiemetic early, and uses plain language with empathy.
Asks the sexual, drug and exposure questions of the travel history sensitively and without judgement, explaining why they are asked.
History
Characterises the vomiting:

kids.x: Onset and duration: sudden, for 2 days
Content: partly digested food, now mostly clear fluid; asks specifically about blood or coffee grounds (none)
Frequency and timing: 3 times yesterday, twice today, not related to meals
Modifying factors and impact: nothing helps or worsens it; barely keeping sips down; missed work yesterday and today

check.x: Elicits the illness since returning and its timeline: malaise and aches from about 10 days ago, fevers and sweats, nausea and loss of appetite.
Characterises the right upper quadrant pain: dull, constant, about 4/10, for 5 days, no radiation, not colicky and not related to fatty food.
Asks specifically about features of liver disease and elicits dark urine and pale stools; asks about jaundice and itch (none).
check.d: Score if dark urine and pale stools are both elicited and jaundice is asked about.

check.x: Asks about features of severe illness: confusion or drowsiness and bleeding or bruising (none), and dehydration (less urine, light-headed on standing).
Screens for other causes of vomiting across at least 2 systems:
check.d: Score the parent if at least 2 sub-boxes, including the non-gastrointestinal one, are earned. Credit any reasonable question for each differential.

kids.x: Obstruction: bowels open and passing wind, no distension, no previous surgery
Biliary and pancreatic: no colicky pain after fatty meals, no epigastric pain through to the back, minimal alcohol
Appendicitis and gastroenteritis: no pain moving to the right iliac fossa, no diarrhoea, no unwell contacts
Peptic, reflux and varices: no heartburn, NSAIDs, haematemesis or melaena, no known liver disease
Non-gastrointestinal: pregnancy (last period, sexual activity), headache or neck stiffness, urinary symptoms, diabetes

check.x: Takes a structured travel history:

kids.x: Where and when: 4 weeks in northern India, including rural villages; returned 3 weeks ago (fits the incubation period)
Food and water: street food, salads, cut fruit, ice, tap water for brushing teeth; hostels and guesthouses
Pre-travel care: no travel consultation, no hepatitis A vaccine, no malaria prophylaxis
Mosquito bites and nets (bitten often, nets only sometimes)
Blood-borne and other exposures: sex, tattoos, piercings, injections, medical or dental care, fresh water, animals, and sick contacts (all negative apart from her friend's brief diarrhoea)

check.x: Takes the past history, medications and allergies: nil past history, no medicines including paracetamol, herbal remedies or supplements, no allergies.
Takes the family and social history: nothing significant in the family; careers adviser, non-smoker, quantifies occasional weekend alcohol, never injected drugs, lives alone.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks she ate something bad, worried it is more serious, wants the vomiting to stop and to know what it is.
Examination
Asks for the full set of vital signs and assesses hydration: HR 104, temperature 37.9 °C, dry mucous membranes, CRT and peripheral perfusion.
Inspects the sclerae and skin for jaundice (none), and looks for stigmata of chronic liver disease, rash, bruising and lymphadenopathy (none).
check.d: Score if the sclerae or skin are inspected for jaundice and at least 2 of: stigmata of chronic liver disease, rash or bruising, lymph nodes.

check.x: Assesses for hepatic encephalopathy: orientation and asterixis (alert, oriented, no asterixis).
Palpates the abdomen systematically: mild RUQ tenderness, a smooth tender liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin, Murphy's sign negative, no guarding or rebound.
Feels for splenomegaly (none), checks the right iliac fossa (not tender) and asks for a urine dipstick (bilirubin 2+, ketones 2+) and a pregnancy test.
check.d: Score if the spleen is palpated and either a urine dipstick or a pregnancy test is requested.

check.x: Interpretation

Interprets the observations: all white zone, but persistent tachycardia (104 to 108) with vomiting, concentrated dark urine (SG 1.030) and reduced urine output by her account means mild volume depletion needing treatment.
Interprets the LFTs as an acute hepatocellular hepatitis: transaminases in the thousands (ALT 2840) with ALP only modestly raised.
States that liver synthetic function is preserved (INR 1.1, normal glucose) and, with her normal mental state, that there is no acute liver failure.
Interprets the other bloods: raised urea (8.6) and low potassium (3.3) from vomiting and poor intake; normal lipase makes pancreatitis unlikely; beta-hCG negative.
Interprets the serology and malaria tests: hepatitis A IgM detected means acute hepatitis A; hepatitis B, C and E negative; one negative malaria antigen and film set does not exclude malaria.
Interprets the ultrasound: no gallstones or duct dilatation (no biliary obstruction); the thick-walled gallbladder without stones or sonographic Murphy's sign fits acute hepatitis, not cholecystitis.

Gives acute hepatitis A as the most likely diagnosis, justified by at least 4 of: returned traveller with unsafe food and water, unvaccinated, prodrome of fever, malaise and anorexia, RUQ pain with a tender liver, dark urine and pale stools, ALT in the thousands, hepatitis A IgM detected.
Gives at least 3 differentials from at least 2 systems, each with a feature for or against it from this case: malaria, cholangitis or cholecystitis, acute pancreatitis, appendicitis, gastroenteritis.
check.d: Also credit hepatitis E, acute hepatitis B, typhoid or drug-induced liver injury with a reason.

check.x: Management

Gives supportive care: IV crystalloid bolus with reassessment, then maintenance with potassium, an antiemetic (e.g. ondansetron 4 mg IV; correct potassium; consider an ECG if giving repeated QT-prolonging antiemetics), a fluid balance chart, and no hepatotoxic drugs or alcohol; states there is no specific antiviral treatment.
check.d: Score if IV fluids with reassessment, potassium replacement, an antiemetic and avoiding hepatotoxic drugs are given.

check.x: Arranges infection control in the ED: a single room with its own toilet, standard precautions with strict hand hygiene (and contact precautions as local policy requires).
Notifies hepatitis A to the local public health unit as a notifiable disease, for contact tracing and prophylaxis.
Excludes malaria properly: repeats films 12 to 24 hours apart until 3 sets are negative, takes blood cultures, and discusses with infectious diseases if any doubt remains.
Plans disposition: short-stay admission until she tolerates oral fluids, repeat LFTs and INR, and escalation to gastroenterology or the liver unit for a rising INR, rising bilirubin or any confusion.

Explains to Leticia in plain words that she has a liver infection caught from contaminated food or water, that it usually settles by itself over weeks and does not become long-term, and checks her understanding.
check.d: Credit whether given in the management or the discharge answer.

check.x: Safety netting

Tells her the red flags in plain words and where to go: confusion or drowsiness, bleeding or bruising, being unable to keep fluids down, worsening pain or yellow skin with fever, fainting; return to ED, or call 000 if confused or collapsing; new or recurring fever, rigors or sweats (possible malaria): return to ED the same day.
check.d: Score if at least 3 red flags are given with where to go.

check.x: Gives infection advice: hand washing after the toilet and before food, no preparing food for others, off work until public health advises, and that public health will offer close contacts hepatitis A vaccine (or normal human immunoglobulin if needed) within 2 weeks of their last exposure.
check.d: Score if hand hygiene, no food preparation for others and contact prophylaxis are given.

check.x: Arranges GP follow-up within 2 to 3 days with repeat LFTs and INR, and makes sure 3 malaria sets are negative before discharge or arranges the remaining films.

part2.lead: Here are Leticia's observations, her blood results, her hepatitis serology and malaria tests, and the ultrasound report.
part2.patient:
While the candidate answers the fourth question, Leticia asks once: "Is it contagious? Could I have given it to someone?"

If the candidate uses jargon (notifiable, serology, immunoglobulin), ask: "What does that mean?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Triage set at 14:10 and the nurse's repeat set at 15:10, both on room air.
handover.model:
• Read: at 14:10, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, BP 112/70, HR 104 and temperature 37.9 °C are all in the white zone, with pain 4/10. At 15:10, HR 108, BP 108/68 and temperature 38.1 °C are still white. She vomited again at 14:30 and has passed about 100 mL of dark urine.
  • Meaning: a persistent tachycardia with ongoing vomiting, poor intake, concentrated dark urine (SG 1.030) and reduced urine output by her account means mild volume depletion. The low-grade fever fits a viral prodrome, but in a traveller back from India it keeps malaria on the list until it is excluded. Nothing triggers a chart call, but a white zone chart does not mean she needs no treatment.
  • Changes: start (or continue, if ordered in Part 1) IV fluids and an antiemetic, with regular observations and a fluid balance chart; a clinical review for any yellow-zone value and a rapid response for any red-zone value or any drowsiness or confusion.

rows.note: Triage ATS 3: vomiting, unwell after overseas travel. IV cannula, bloods sent
Vomited about 150 mL clear fluid at 14:30. Passed about 100 mL dark urine

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Leticia Moreno. Collected 14:15 at cannulation. Sample not haemolysed. No previous results on file.
handover.model:
• Read: ALT 2840 and AST 1910 with ALP 168 and GGT 142 only modestly raised; bilirubin 38, mostly conjugated. INR 1.1 and glucose 5.4 normal (albumin 39 is also normal, but with a half-life of about 3 weeks it does not reflect acute synthetic function). Urea 8.6 raised with normal creatinine; potassium 3.3 low. Lipase normal. WCC, neutrophils, lymphocytes and platelets normal; CRP 14 mildly raised. Beta-hCG below 2.
  • Meaning: a hepatocellular pattern with transaminases in the thousands is an acute hepatitis (viral, drug or ischaemic); she takes no medicines and is not shocked, so viral is most likely. The conjugated bilirubin explains the dark urine and pale stools. A normal INR, glucose and mental state mean no acute liver failure. Raised urea and low potassium reflect vomiting and poor intake. Normal lipase makes pancreatitis unlikely. Normal platelets count against malaria and dengue but do not exclude malaria. She is not pregnant.
  • Changes: IV fluids with potassium; repeat UEC, LFTs and INR; avoid hepatotoxic drugs.

handover.label: Hepatitis serology and malaria tests
handover.result: Collected 14:15. Hepatitis A IgM result phoned to the ED at 16:40 (urgent on-site serology). Malaria: first set only. Laboratory comment: a single negative set does not exclude malaria; repeat films at 12 to 24 hour intervals if clinically indicated.
handover.model:
• Read: hepatitis A IgM detected. Hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis B core antibody, hepatitis C antibody and hepatitis E IgM not detected. Malaria antigen not detected and no parasites on the first thick and thin films.
  • Meaning: a positive hepatitis A IgM confirms acute hepatitis A, which fits the travel, the absent vaccination, the timing and the LFTs. Hepatitis B, C and E are not the cause. One negative malaria set does not exclude malaria in a febrile traveller from India who took no prophylaxis.
  • Changes: notify the public health unit; supportive care; infection control; repeat malaria films 12 to 24 hours apart until 3 sets are negative.

handover.label: Upper abdominal ultrasound
handover.result:
Examination: ultrasound of the upper abdomen (liver, gallbladder, biliary tree, pancreas, spleen and kidneys), 16:10.

Clinical details: 35-year-old woman, returned from India 3 weeks ago. About 10 days of malaise, fever and anorexia; RUQ pain for 5 days; dark urine and pale stools; vomiting for 2 days. ALT 2840 U/L, bilirubin 38 µmol/L. ?Hepatitis ?Biliary obstruction.

Findings:

  • Liver: mildly enlarged, 17 cm in the midclavicular line. Mildly reduced echogenicity throughout. Smooth outline. No focal lesion. Portal vein patent with normal direction of flow; hepatic veins patent.
  • Gallbladder: contracted, with a diffusely thickened, layered and oedematous wall measuring 7 mm. No gallstones or sludge. Sonographic Murphy's sign negative. No pericholecystic collection.
  • Bile ducts: common bile duct 3 mm. No intrahepatic or extrahepatic duct dilatation. No duct calculus seen.
  • Pancreas: normal size and echotexture. No peripancreatic fluid.
  • Spleen: normal size, 11 cm.
  • Kidneys: normal size, no hydronephrosis.
  • Other: no ascites. No pleural effusion.

Conclusion: mild hepatomegaly with a contracted, thick-walled gallbladder without gallstones or a sonographic Murphy's sign, a pattern seen in acute hepatitis. No biliary dilatation and no focal liver lesion. Normal spleen and pancreas.
handover.model:
• Read: a mildly enlarged liver with reduced echogenicity and no focal lesion; patent portal and hepatic veins. A contracted gallbladder with a 7 mm oedematous wall, no stones or sludge, and a negative sonographic Murphy's sign. CBD 3 mm with no duct dilatation. Normal pancreas and spleen, no ascites.
  • Meaning: no biliary obstruction, so the pale stools and dark urine come from cholestasis within the liver. Gallbladder wall thickening is common in acute hepatitis and, without stones or a sonographic Murphy's sign, is not cholecystitis. A normal spleen counts against malaria and typhoid but does not exclude them. Patent hepatic veins exclude Budd-Chiari syndrome.
  • Changes: no surgical referral or ERCP is needed; continue supportive care for acute hepatitis.

ask: You are now calling the medical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Leticia Moreno, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Leticia now, here in the emergency department.
Before Leticia goes home, what would you tell her and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Leticia Moreno, 35.
  • Situation: acute hepatitis A with dehydration from vomiting; no acute liver failure; requesting short-stay admission.
  • Background: 4 weeks in India, back 3 weeks; unvaccinated, no malaria prophylaxis, street food; 10-day prodrome, RUQ pain, dark urine, pale stools, 2 days of vomiting; no medicines.
  • Assessment: HR 104 rising to 108, T 38.1 °C, all white zone, but persistent tachycardia, dry mucosa and concentrated urine mean mild volume depletion. LFTs show an acute hepatocellular hepatitis: ALT 2840 (more than 50 × ULN) with ALP and GGT only modestly raised, conjugated bilirubin 26. No acute liver failure: INR 1.1, glucose 5.4, alert, no asterixis. Urea 8.6 and K 3.3 from vomiting; normal lipase, so pancreatitis unlikely; beta-hCG negative. HAV IgM detected means acute hepatitis A; B, C and E negative. First malaria set negative, but one set does not exclude malaria. Ultrasound: no stones or duct dilatation, so no obstruction; thick gallbladder wall fits hepatitis, not cholecystitis.
  • Recommendation: IV fluids and antiemetic started; please review for admission; I have notified public health; repeat malaria films and LFTs/INR.

Acute hepatitis A: unvaccinated traveller with unsafe food and water, onset within the incubation period, prodrome of fever, malaise and anorexia, RUQ pain and tender liver, dark urine and pale stools, ALT 2840, HAV IgM detected.

  • Malaria (must not miss): for: fever, India, no prophylaxis, bites; against: normal platelets and spleen, first set negative; needs 3 sets.
  • Cholangitis or cholecystitis: for: fever, RUQ pain, pale stools; against: not colicky, Murphy's negative, no stones, CBD 3 mm, hepatocellular LFTs.
  • Acute pancreatitis: against: lipase normal, no back pain, minimal alcohol.
  • Appendicitis: against: no right iliac fossa pain.
  • Gastroenteritis: for: food and water exposure; against: no diarrhoea, LFTs.

1. Fluids: IV crystalloid bolus (e.g. 1 L 0.9% sodium chloride or Hartmann's), reassess, then maintenance with potassium (premixed bag, or oral once tolerated); fluid balance chart, urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/h (about 30 mL/h).
  2. Antiemetic: ondansetron 4 mg IV (correct potassium; consider an ECG if giving repeated QT-prolonging antiemetics); no hepatotoxic drugs, no alcohol; no specific antiviral treatment.
  3. Analgesia if needed (not scored): paracetamol at a reduced dose (e.g. no more than 2 g/day while LFTs are this high); avoid NSAIDs.
  4. Infection control: single room with own toilet, standard precautions, strict hand hygiene.
  5. Notify the local public health unit.
  6. Malaria: repeat films 12 to 24 hours apart until 3 negative; blood cultures; ID advice if doubt.
  7. Disposition: short-stay admission until tolerating fluids; repeat LFTs and INR; escalate to gastroenterology or the liver unit if INR or bilirubin rising or any confusion.

• Plain words: a liver infection from contaminated food or water; it usually settles over weeks and does not become long-term; tiredness may last weeks; your eyes or skin may turn yellow over the next few days, which is expected; come back if it is with fever, confusion or bleeding; checks her understanding (teach-back).
  • Red flags: confusion or drowsiness, bleeding or bruising, unable to keep fluids down, worsening pain or yellowing with fever, fainting: return to ED; call 000 if confused or collapsing. New or recurring fever, rigors or sweats (possible malaria): return to ED the same day.
  • Infection: wash hands after the toilet and before food, don't prepare food for others; off work until public health advises.
  • Contacts: it spreads through hands and food; public health will contact the people close to you and offer them a vaccine (or an antibody injection) if it is within 2 weeks of contact.
  • Follow-up: GP in 2 to 3 days for repeat LFTs and INR; confirm 3 negative malaria sets before discharge, or arrange the remaining films the next day with the result followed up.

ddx.for: An unvaccinated traveller who ate street food, salads and ice in India, with a prodrome of fever, malaise and anorexia, RUQ pain, a tender liver, dark urine, pale stools, ALT 2840 and hepatitis A IgM detected.
Fever after travel to rural India with frequent mosquito bites, inconsistent nets and no malaria prophylaxis.
ddx.against: Normal platelets and spleen, a negative first antigen test and film set, and a confirmed alternative diagnosis, though 3 negative sets are still needed.

ddx.dx: Acute cholangitis or acute calculous cholecystitis
ddx.for: Fever, RUQ pain, pale stools, dark urine and a thick-walled gallbladder on ultrasound.
ddx.against: The pain is a dull constant ache rather than colic, Murphy's sign is negative, there are no gallstones and the CBD is 3 mm, and the LFTs are hepatocellular.
No epigastric pain through to the back, minimal alcohol, normal lipase and a normal pancreas on ultrasound.
The pain is in the right upper quadrant and has not moved, the right iliac fossa is not tender, and the illness has lasted 10 days.

ddx.for: Unsafe food and water exposure and a friend with brief diarrhoea on the trip.
ddx.against: No diarrhoea at any time, symptoms began after her return, and the LFTs show a marked hepatitis.

guide:
In Part 1, Leticia gives each detail only when asked. The travel details in particular come only to specific questions. The examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The nurse reports the further vomit partway through. If the candidate orders any other treatment in Part 1, say "Noted, please cover it in Part 2". An antiemetic or IV fluids ordered in Part 1 are given; credit the antiemetic under item 3 and still expect fluids to be described in Part 2. If they ask for blood results, serology, malaria tests or imaging, say these will come in Part 2.

In Part 2, hand over the observations, the bloods, the serology and malaria tests, and the ultrasound report, then ask all four questions in order. Leticia asks her one question while the candidate answers the fourth question.

A high-performing candidate characterises the vomiting and the illness since her return, asks specifically about dark urine, pale stools and jaundice, and takes a structured travel history including vaccination, malaria prophylaxis, food and water, bites and blood-borne exposures. They examine for jaundice, encephalopathy, a tender liver and splenomegaly. In Part 2 they read a hepatocellular hepatitis with preserved synthetic function, confirm hepatitis A on serology, say one negative malaria set is not enough, and read the gallbladder wall as part of the hepatitis. They rehydrate, notify public health, arrange infection control and repeat malaria films, and give clear advice on hygiene, contacts, work and follow-up.

A borderline candidate takes a vomiting history but asks little about the trip or vaccines, misses the dark urine and pale stools, or does not check for encephalopathy. They may call the ultrasound cholecystitis, treat the INR as irrelevant, or forget notification and malaria. A failing candidate calls it gastroenteritis and discharges her with oral fluids.
explain:
Diagnosis: acute hepatitis A

Leticia spent 4 weeks backpacking in northern India. She ate street food, salads, cut fruit and ice, and had no travel vaccines. About a week and a half after returning she developed the typical prodrome of acute viral hepatitis: malaise, aches, fever, nausea and anorexia. Then came right upper quadrant pain, dark urine and pale stools, and finally vomiting. Her symptoms began about 11 days after she returned. Her trip ran from about 5.5 to 1.5 weeks before symptom onset. Hepatitis A has an incubation period of about 15 to 50 days (typically around 4 weeks), which fits exposure during the first 3 or so weeks of her trip. Hepatitis A spreads by the faecal-oral route through contaminated food and water. It is endemic in much of South Asia, and unvaccinated travellers are at risk. Infection in adults is usually symptomatic and often causes jaundice. She has not yet become visibly jaundiced, but her conjugated bilirubin is raised.

Hepatitis A does not become chronic. Most people recover fully over weeks, although fatigue can last longer and a minority have a relapse. Acute liver failure is rare but is the complication that matters, and the risk is higher in older adults and people with chronic liver disease.

Taking the history: vomiting in a returned traveller

Characterise the vomiting (onset, content including blood or coffee grounds, frequency, relation to meals) and then look for its cause across more than one system. Here the clues are the illness that came before the vomiting and the dark urine and pale stools, which patients rarely volunteer. Screen for obstruction, biliary and pancreatic disease, appendicitis, peptic disease and gastroenteritis, and for causes outside the gut: pregnancy, raised intracranial pressure, urinary infection and diabetic ketoacidosis.

A travel history covers:

  • When she returned, to match against incubation periods.
  • Where she went, urban or rural.
  • Accommodation: hostels, mosquito nets.
  • Activities: unprotected sex, fresh water, animals.
  • Food and drink: bottled or tap water, ice, street food, raw food and salads.
  • Pre-travel vaccines and prophylaxis, and whether she took them as directed.
  • Sick contacts, insect bites, tattoos and piercings, and any medical or dental treatment abroad.

Differentials that matter

  • Malaria: treat any fever in a traveller back from a malaria-endemic area as malaria until proven otherwise. India has both P. vivax and P. falciparum, and Leticia took no prophylaxis. One negative set does not exclude it. Repeat thick and thin films (with an antigen test) 12 to 24 hours apart until 3 sets are negative.
  • Other viral hepatitis: hepatitis E is also spread by food and water in South Asia and gives the same picture. Acute hepatitis B needs blood or sexual exposure. Serology separates them.
  • Typhoid fever: fever in a traveller from South Asia, so take blood cultures.
  • Biliary disease: cholangitis and cholecystitis cause fever, RUQ pain and cholestasis. Ultrasound finds no stones and no duct dilatation.
  • Pancreatitis, appendicitis and gastroenteritis: each made unlikely by the features above.
  • Drug-induced liver injury, including paracetamol: always ask about prescribed, over-the-counter and herbal medicines. Leticia takes none.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: all values are in the white zone, but a persistent tachycardia with vomiting, concentrated dark urine (SG 1.030) and reduced urine output by her account means volume depletion.
  • LFTs: transaminases in the thousands with a relatively modest ALP and GGT is a hepatocellular pattern. The main causes are viral hepatitis, drugs (especially paracetamol) and ischaemia. Cholestasis within the liver causes the conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, the dark urine (bilirubin on the dipstick) and the pale stools.
  • Synthetic function: the INR, glucose and conscious state matter more than the height of the ALT. A normal INR and glucose with a normal mental state mean there is no acute liver failure. A rising INR or any encephalopathy needs urgent specialist (liver unit) discussion.
  • Serology: hepatitis A IgM detected means acute infection. Hepatitis B, C and E are negative.
  • Ultrasound: it excludes biliary obstruction and focal lesions. A thick, oedematous gallbladder wall is common in acute hepatitis. Without stones or a sonographic Murphy's sign it must not be mistaken for cholecystitis.

Management

  • Supportive care: there is no specific antiviral treatment. Give IV fluids for dehydration with potassium replacement, an antiemetic and a fluid balance chart.
  • Medicines: avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic drugs, and review any medicine against her liver function.
  • Analgesia if needed: paracetamol at a reduced dose (e.g. no more than 2 g/day while LFTs are this high); avoid NSAIDs.
  • Admission and monitoring: she cannot keep fluids down and lives alone, so a short-stay admission is reasonable. Repeat LFTs and INR, and escalate if the INR or bilirubin rises or confusion develops.
  • Infection control: a single room with its own toilet, standard precautions and strict hand hygiene.
  • Exclude malaria with repeat films, and take blood cultures.

Public health

Hepatitis A is notifiable in every Australian state and territory. Notify the local public health unit promptly; the laboratory also notifies. The public health unit:

  • traces close contacts (household, sexual, and anyone who ate food she prepared) during the infectious period, which runs from about 2 weeks before symptom onset until 1 week after jaundice starts, or 2 weeks after symptom onset if there is no jaundice (CDNA);
  • offers contacts post-exposure prophylaxis within 2 weeks of their last exposure, as the Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends: hepatitis A vaccine, or normal human immunoglobulin for those who cannot be vaccinated or are at higher risk;
  • advises on excluding her from food handling and work, and from caring for children, patients or older people, until she is no longer infectious.

Advise careful hand washing after the toilet and before handling food, no preparing food for others, and separate towels. The Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends hepatitis A vaccination for travellers to endemic areas. She is now immune, but future trips still need a pre-travel consultation, including malaria prophylaxis.

Safety netting

Leticia returns to the ED for:

  • confusion or drowsiness, unusual bleeding or bruising (possible liver failure);
  • vomiting so that she cannot keep fluids down, or fainting;
  • worsening pain, or deepening jaundice with fever;
  • new or recurring fever, rigors or sweats (possible malaria): return to ED the same day.

She or someone with her calls 000 if she becomes confused or collapses. Before discharge, make sure 3 malaria sets are negative, or arrange the remaining films the next day with the result followed up. She sees her GP within 2 to 3 days for repeat LFTs and INR until they are clearly improving, avoids alcohol until her liver tests are normal, and stays off work until public health says she can return.

Every returned traveller needs a structured travel history: when and where, accommodation, food and water, activities and sex, bites, tattoos and procedures, sick contacts, and pre-travel vaccines and prophylaxis.
Transaminases in the thousands are a hepatocellular hepatitis (viral, drug or ischaemic). Judge severity by the INR, glucose and mental state, not the height of the ALT.
Any fever after travel to a malaria-endemic area is malaria until proven otherwise. One negative set is not enough; repeat films 12 to 24 hours apart until 3 are negative.
Hepatitis A is managed supportively and does not become chronic, but it is notifiable. Public health traces contacts and offers vaccine or immunoglobulin within 2 weeks of exposure.
